seo_description: Psychological horror game about dementia and memory. Solo audio designer — built footstep detection, enemy proximity, anomaly systems, and dynamic music in Wwise + UE5 + C++.
hero.title: Shadow Frames
hero.subtitle: An old man with dementia. An abandoned pub. Sounds that won't let him forget.
concept.hook: I picked this project because horror sound design is where creativity has no limits. Four months as the sole audio designer on the team.
concept.p1: Shadow Frames is a psychological horror about an elderly man with dementia. He wanders through an abandoned 1960s Irish pub — entirely in black and white — where anomalies keep appearing. Levitating glasses, drifting shadows, spinning chairs. Each one is a fragment of memory: his son, his daughter, moments from years ago. The anomalies pull him deeper into nostalgia and grief. At the end, he finds his son hooked up to an IV, drinking. Beyond saving. He calls an ambulance, and the game just... stops. You don't find out what happens.
concept.p2: There's no HUD, no markers, nothing on screen pointing you anywhere. Sound is the only way to find anomalies. Mute the game and you're blind. Every creak, whisper, and rattle carries directional information. You follow the sound, photograph the anomaly, pin it to a board, and piece the story together.
concept.p3: This was a multi-school collaboration: our game dev team at Howest DAE, a writer from RITCS working on her master's, and a composer from the Royal Conservatory of Ghent, also finishing her master's. I wrote a Sound Bible — a full document describing how every sound in the game should work, so anyone joining the project could get up to speed. I also built the dynamic music system around the stems the composer sent me.
systems.footstep.title: Footstep Detection
systems.footstep.desc: The pub has wood floors, tiles, concrete, and creaky boards. A physics line-trace fires downward from the player's feet each step — the Physical Material from the hit maps to a Wwise Switch. Level designers add new surfaces in the editor without touching code.
systems.proximity.title: Enemy Proximity
systems.proximity.desc: There's always an enemy somewhere in the pub, stalking you. As it gets closer, layers of dread ambience and stressed breathing fade in through RTPC. I used a hysteresis state machine with dual thresholds (start at 70%, stop at 60%) so the audio doesn't flicker when the enemy hovers near the boundary.
systems.anomaly.title: Anomaly System
systems.anomaly.desc: Each anomaly has three audio stages: an alert burst when it spawns, a directional hint so you can track it down, and a sustained presence loop until you photograph it. Every anomaly sounds different. The camera shutter sound is different too. Spatial audio cues are the only way to find them — there's nothing on screen.

code.title: Technical Deep Dive
code.hint: 3 annotated C++ snippets. Click lines with dots for explanations
challenge1.title: Audio Flickering at Proximity Boundaries
challenge1.hard: Early on, when the enemy hovered near the proximity trigger boundary, the dread audio toggled on and off every single frame. Players heard a horrible machine-gun stutter instead of smooth tension building. It completely broke the mood.
challenge1.did: I built a hysteresis state machine with separate start (70%) and stop (60%) thresholds. That 10% gap means the audio can't flicker at the boundary. RTPC handles smooth intensity transitions. Problem gone.
challenge2.title: Surface Detection Without Per-Level Setup
challenge2.hard: The pub has four floor materials. We started by tagging surfaces manually per level, but it was painfully slow and broke every time the level designer moved geometry around. Nobody wanted to maintain it.
challenge2.did: I switched to Unreal's Physical Material system with line traces. Each physics material maps automatically to a Wwise Switch. Designers add new surfaces in the editor — no code changes, no per-level tagging. It just works.
